questions.q: What makes 'Which customers are most likely to leave, and what one action could reduce churn?' a good capstone question?
options: It is vague enough to allow any analysis
It asks for every possible chart
It requires building a deep learning model
It is specific, ends in a decision, and the data can plausibly speak to it
questions.explain: A good question is specific and ties to a decision. Otherwise exploration becomes a tour of every column.

questions.q: Why does the capstone use a seeded, generated dataset in this walkthrough?
options: Real data can never be used in a portfolio
So every number is reproducible; the workflow then transfers to a real dataset you choose
Because generated data is always more accurate
Because pandas cannot read files
questions.explain: A fixed seed makes results checkable. The steps are the same for a real dataset in your own portfolio version.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call the generator script an 'answer key'?
options: Real data comes with no recipe, so try the analysis first and compare with the recipe only at the end
It contains the quiz answers
It encrypts the dataset
It is required to run pandas
questions.explain: In real work you never see how the data was generated. Peeking early would spoil the exercise.

questions.q: In the first look, 157 of 800 customers churned. What is the baseline churn rate?
options: 157 percent
8 percent
About 19.6 percent, roughly one customer in five
About 80 percent

questions.q: Why establish the baseline churn rate before comparing groups?
options: Because groups cannot be compared without a model
So each group's rate can be judged against the overall rate
Because baselines are needed to make charts colorful
Baselines are optional and unrelated to interpretation
questions.explain: A rate like 26 percent only means something relative to the overall 19.6 percent.
